subject: ela
intro: Each problem includes a full passage that follows a story from its beginning through its resolution. Read the whole passage carefully, then trace how the character changes, how the conflict develops, and how the setting and episodes work together. Support every answer with evidence from several places in the text.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer the question.

When the science fair sign-up sheet went around, Maya kept her hands flat on her desk. Last year her volcano had fizzled in front of the whole gym, and the memory still made her ears burn. She decided she would skip the fair this time and nobody would notice.

But Mr. Okafor noticed the blank line where her name should be. He did not push. Instead, he handed her a battered notebook full of his own failed experiments, the pages crossed out and re-tried in three different colors of ink. "Every one of these is a flop," he said. "That is how I learned anything."

Maya took the notebook home and read it twice. The next morning she wrote her name on the sheet, but small, in the corner, as if she could still take it back. For two weeks she built a model of a water filter, testing it again and again. The first version leaked. The second clogged. By the third, she stopped flinching when something went wrong and just wrote down what happened.

On the day of the fair, her filter ran cloudy water clear in front of the judges. One judge asked what she would change next time, and instead of freezing, Maya pulled out her own notebook, now full of crossed-out lines, and walked him through every failure. She did not win first place. But walking home, she realized she was already planning version four.

Trace how Maya changes from the beginning of the story to the resolution, and identify the turning point that begins her change. Use evidence from the text.
items.answer: At the beginning Maya is so afraid of failing again that she plans to skip the fair entirely, keeping her hands flat and her name off the sheet. By the resolution she treats failure as part of the process: she calmly walks a judge through her crossed-out failures and is already planning version four. The turning point is when Mr. Okafor gives her his notebook of failed experiments and says that is how he learned anything, which reframes failure as a tool rather than a humiliation.

steps: Find Maya at the start: she 'kept her hands flat,' the volcano memory 'made her ears burn,' and she 'decided she would skip the fair.' She is avoiding the fair out of fear of failing.
Find Maya at the end: she does not freeze when a judge questions her, she 'walked him through every failure,' and she is 'already planning version four.' She now accepts failure as useful.
Locate the turning point: Mr. Okafor hands her his notebook of flops and says, 'That is how I learned anything.' This is the event that makes her sign up and keep testing.
Connect the change to its cause: the notebook reframes failure, so contrast the fearful beginning with the confident ending and name the notebook moment as the cause of the change.

Read the passage, then answer the question.

The ferry to Gull Island ran only twice a day, and Devon had just watched the morning boat pull away from the dock without him. His grandmother's house key was in his pocket, but the house was across the water, and now he had six hours to wait.

He slumped onto a bench by the harbor. At first he was furious at himself. He had stopped to photograph a heron and lost track of time, and the missed boat felt like proof that he ruined everything by getting distracted. He almost called his mother to come get him, ready to give up on the visit entirely.

Instead, with nothing else to do, he started walking the harbor road. He found a small museum about the island's lighthouse keepers and spent an hour reading their logbooks. An old keeper had written about waiting out storms, sometimes for days, with no boat in or out. Devon copied a line into his phone: "The waiting is part of the keeping."

When he came out, he noticed the light on the water had turned gold, and he photographed the empty harbor. By the time the afternoon ferry arrived, Devon was almost sorry to leave the dock. On the crossing he told his grandmother he had missed the morning boat, but he said it like a story, not a confession. He had stopped seeing the delay as a failure.

Explain how the setting of the harbor shapes Devon's change, and identify the event that turns his frustration into something else. Use evidence from the text.
items.answer: The harbor setting traps Devon with six hours and nothing to do, which forces him to walk the harbor road instead of leaving, and it offers the museum and the golden light that change his mood. The turning event is reading the lighthouse keeper's logbook line, 'The waiting is part of the keeping,' which reframes the long wait as meaningful rather than as proof that he ruins everything. By the resolution the same delay he once saw as a failure becomes a story he tells without shame.

steps: Identify the setting's role: the ferry 'ran only twice a day' and the house is 'across the water,' so the harbor strands Devon and gives him six empty hours.
Note Devon's starting state: he is 'furious at himself' and feels the missed boat is 'proof that he ruined everything.'
Find the turning event the setting provides: the harbor museum and the keeper's line 'The waiting is part of the keeping,' which he copies down.

Connect setting, event, and change: because the harbor confines him, he finds the museum and the line, and by the end he tells the missed boat 'like a story, not a confession.' The setting drives the shift in how he sees the delay.

Read the passage, then answer the question.

Rosa had captained the robotics team for two years, and she ran every meeting the same way: she decided, the others built. It was efficient, and they had the trophies to prove it. So when their new robot kept tipping over on the test ramp three days before the state competition, Rosa did what she always did. She told everyone exactly how to fix it. They obeyed. The robot still tipped.

That night, frustrated, she stayed late and overheard two teammates in the hallway. "She never asks us anything," one said. "I had an idea about the weight, but what's the point?" Rosa stood very still. She had assumed their silence meant agreement.

The next morning she did something that felt almost painful: she set down her clipboard and asked the team what they thought was wrong. At first no one spoke. Then the teammate from the hallway mentioned moving the battery lower to drop the center of gravity. Another suggested widening the base. Rosa wanted to overrule both ideas, but she made herself say, "Let's try it."

They rebuilt the robot together, arguing and adjusting all afternoon. On the test ramp, it held steady. At the state competition two days later they placed second, their best finish ever, and when a judge asked Rosa about her leadership, she said the robot was the whole team's design. She did not mention the clipboard she had finally put down.

Trace how Rosa changes across the story, and identify the moment that prompts the change. Be careful to name the actual cause. Use evidence from the text.
items.answer: At the start Rosa leads by command: 'she decided, the others built,' and she fixes the tipping robot by telling everyone exactly what to do. By the resolution she leads by listening, asking the team what is wrong, trying their ideas, and crediting 'the whole team's design.' The moment that prompts the change is overhearing her teammates in the hallway say, 'She never asks us anything,' which shatters her assumption that their silence meant agreement and makes her put down the clipboard.

steps: Establish Rosa's beginning: 'she decided, the others built,' and she responds to the tipping robot by telling everyone 'exactly how to fix it.'
Establish Rosa's ending: she asks the team for ideas, says 'Let's try it,' and credits 'the whole team's design.'
Find the true turning point: overhearing 'She never asks us anything' and realizing she 'had assumed their silence meant agreement.'
Avoid the wrong cause: the second-place finish is a result of the change, not its cause. The hallway conversation is what actually prompts her to set down the clipboard.

Read the passage, then answer the question.

The blackout hit the apartment building at dusk, right as eleven-year-old Theo was supposed to be watching his little sister, Pip, while their mother worked a late shift. Theo hated the dark. He always slept with the hall light on, and now the whole building was swallowed in it.

Pip, who was five, started to cry. Theo's first instinct was to freeze, his own heart hammering. But Pip's crying got louder, and something in him decided that one scared person in the apartment was enough. He made his voice steady. "It's an adventure," he told her, even though his hands were shaking. "We're explorers and the power is the cave."

He felt his way to the kitchen drawer, found a flashlight, and clicked it on. The small circle of light made the apartment feel smaller and safer. He set Pip up with the flashlight as their "lantern" and they built a fort out of couch cushions. He told her a story about explorers who weren't afraid of caves, and slowly her hiccupping stopped.

When the lights flickered back on two hours later, Pip was asleep against his shoulder. Theo realized he had not thought about being scared in over an hour. He still didn't love the dark. But he had learned he could be steady for someone even when he wasn't steady inside, and that felt like a different kind of brave.

A reader says, "Theo's change is that he stopped being afraid of the dark." Explain why that reading is inaccurate, and describe what actually changes in Theo and what causes it. Use evidence from the text.
items.answer: The reading is inaccurate because the text says Theo 'still didn't love the dark,' so his fear does not disappear. What actually changes is his ability to act steady for someone else despite still being afraid: he makes his voice steady 'even though his hands were shaking' and learns he 'could be steady for someone even when he wasn't steady inside.' The cause is Pip's crying, which makes him decide that 'one scared person in the apartment was enough' and choose to comfort her.

steps: Test the reader's claim against the text: the passage explicitly says 'He still didn't love the dark,' so the fear is not gone.
Identify the real change: Theo learns to act calm for someone else while still afraid, shown by his shaking hands and steady voice and the line about being 'a different kind of brave.'
Find the cause: Pip's louder crying makes him decide 'one scared person in the apartment was enough,' prompting him to comfort her.
Explain the distinction: this is a hard item because it tests whether the student separates a lasting change in behavior from the surface idea that the fear simply ended.

Read the passage, then answer the question.

The drought had lasted all summer, and the creek behind the Alvarez farm had shrunk to a thread. Marisol's job each morning was to carry water to the orchard her grandfather had planted before she was born. She resented it. The trees were old and gnarled and barely fruiting, and hauling buckets in the heat felt pointless. More than once she thought about pouring the water out and saying the trees were already dead.

One morning she found her grandfather sitting under the largest tree, too tired now to climb the hill himself. He didn't scold her for being late. He just told her how he had carried water up that same hill when he was her age, during a drought worse than this one, and how the trees had survived because someone kept showing up.

Marisol didn't answer, but the next morning she carried two buckets instead of one. She started noticing things: which trees drank the most, where the soil cracked first. She began digging small channels so the water reached the roots instead of running off. The work was still hard, but it stopped feeling pointless.

When the first rain finally came in September, the orchard was still alive, every tree. Her grandfather walked the rows slowly, touching the bark. He told her the orchard was hers now. Marisol, who had wanted to pour the water out in July, found that she could not imagine letting a single tree go.

Explain how the drought setting drives the conflict and Marisol's change, and identify the turning point. Use evidence from the text.
items.answer: The drought shrinks the creek 'to a thread' and makes Marisol's daily water-hauling feel pointless, which creates the conflict between her resentment and the dying orchard. Her change is from wanting to 'pour the water out' to being unable 'to imagine letting a single tree go,' shown by her carrying two buckets and digging channels. The turning point is her grandfather telling her how he carried water during a worse drought and that the trees survived 'because someone kept showing up,' which gives her work meaning.

steps: Connect setting to conflict: the drought shrinks the creek and makes the watering chore feel 'pointless,' so the drought is the source of Marisol's resentment.
Track the beginning attitude: she 'thought about pouring the water out' and saying the trees were dead.
Find the turning point: her grandfather's story that the trees survived 'because someone kept showing up.'
Track the ending: she carries two buckets, digs channels, and cannot 'imagine letting a single tree go.' The drought setting and the grandfather's words together drive her change.

Read the passage, then answer the question.

Kai had begged for the lead role in the school play for three years, and finally, as a sixth grader, he got it. Then, the week before opening night, the auditorium flooded. A pipe had burst overnight, and the stage floor buckled. The principal announced the play would be cancelled.

Kai's first reaction was to be angry at the building, the pipe, the bad luck. He sat in the wrecked auditorium and stared at the warped boards. But then he noticed the drama teacher, Ms. Lin, quietly stacking the salvaged costumes, not giving up, just sorting what could be saved. Something about that made him stand up.

He started making calls. He asked the gym teacher if they could use the gym. He convinced classmates to build a simple platform stage. He talked the cast, half of whom had already gone home discouraged, into one more rehearsal. It was not the show he had imagined. There were no real lights, just borrowed lamps, and the audience sat on bleachers.

Opening night, the gym was packed. The play went on. Afterward, a younger student asked Kai how he had gotten everyone to come back together. Kai thought about it. "I didn't want to," he admitted. "I wanted to be mad. But staying mad wasn't going to put on a play." He realized he had spent three years wanting the role and only now understood what the role had asked of him.

Identify which event functions as the climax of this story, and explain why, distinguishing it from the flood. Use evidence from the text.
items.answer: The climax is the moment Kai stands up and decides to act, beginning to make calls and organize an alternate show after seeing Ms. Lin sorting the salvaged costumes. This is the climax because it is the turning point where the central conflict (whether the play will happen) shifts toward resolution and where Kai's character changes from angry and stuck to active and responsible. The flood is the inciting problem that creates the conflict, not the climax, because it comes early and only sets up the tension rather than turning it.

steps: Define the conflict: whether the cancelled play can still happen, and whether Kai will stay angry or act.
Locate the climax: 'Something about that made him stand up,' followed by 'He started making calls.' This is the high point where the conflict turns toward a solution.
Distinguish the flood: the burst pipe and cancellation happen early and create the problem, so they are the inciting event or start of the conflict, not the turning point.
Justify with character: the climax is also where Kai changes from wanting 'to be mad' to taking charge, confirming it as the turning point of the arc.

Read the passage, then answer the question.

For as long as anyone could remember, Nadia had been the fast one. She won every race at recess, every relay in gym. Her speed was simply who she was. So when a new student named Beck transferred in and beat her in the fifty-meter dash on his very first day, Nadia laughed it off, sure it was a fluke. The next day Beck beat her again. And the next.

Nadia stopped laughing. She started running alone after school, pushing harder, but Beck only got faster too. She grew short with her friends and snapped at her little brother. She did not recognize the sour feeling that had moved into her chest.

Then, at the district meet, Beck pulled up halfway through his race, clutching his hamstring, and limped off the track. Nadia won by default. She stood at the finish line with the ribbon, waiting to feel like herself again. She didn't. The win felt like nothing.

That evening she found Beck icing his leg outside the locker room. She almost walked past. Instead she sat down and asked how bad it was. They ended up talking for an hour, not about racing, about everything else. Walking home, Nadia noticed the sour feeling was gone. She still wanted to win. But she had stopped needing to be the only fast one, and somehow that felt like more room to breathe.

Trace Nadia's internal change across the story and identify the event that actually resolves it. Be careful not to credit the wrong event. Use evidence from the text.
items.answer: Nadia changes from defining herself entirely by being 'the fast one' to no longer 'needing to be the only fast one,' which leaves her 'more room to breathe.' The event that actually resolves her conflict is sitting down to talk with Beck for an hour about everything but racing, after which the 'sour feeling was gone.' Winning by default at the district meet does not resolve it, because the win 'felt like nothing' and she still did not feel like herself, showing the real change comes from connecting with Beck, not from beating him.

steps: Identify the beginning self-concept: Nadia's 'speed was simply who she was'; being fastest is her identity.
Identify the false resolution: winning by default leaves the win feeling 'like nothing,' so the medal does not fix the sour feeling.
Find the true resolution: talking with Beck for an hour, after which 'the sour feeling was gone.'
State the change and avoid the wrong cause: she stops 'needing to be the only fast one' because of the conversation, not because she won the race.

Read the passage, then answer the question.

The family's move to the city had taken everything familiar from Amir at once: his old street, his friends, the wide quiet sky of the countryside. Now their apartment looked out on a brick wall, and the constant traffic noise made it hard to sleep. He decided he hated the city and made a private plan to be miserable until they moved back.

For weeks he kept that plan. He came straight home from school, refused to explore, and answered his mother's questions with one word. The city stayed loud and gray, exactly as he had decided it would be.

Then one Saturday the building's power went out, and his mother sent him up to the roof to see if the neighbors knew anything. Amir had never been to the roof. When he pushed open the door, he stopped. The whole city spread out below him, and above it, somehow, was a sky just as wide as the one back home, turning pink at the edges. An older neighbor was up there too, watering a row of tomato plants in buckets. "You can grow anything up here," she said. "You just have to come up and look."

Amir started going to the roof most evenings. He helped with the tomatoes. He began noticing things at street level too, a bakery, a chess game in the park. He still missed the countryside. But by spring, when his father mentioned a chance to move back, Amir was surprised to feel his stomach drop. The city had quietly become a place he did not want to leave.

Explain how the setting both creates Amir's conflict and resolves it, and identify the turning point. Use evidence from the text.
items.answer: The city setting creates Amir's conflict by taking 'everything familiar' and replacing it with a brick wall and traffic noise, which makes him decide to hate the city and 'be miserable.' The same setting resolves the conflict through the rooftop, where he finds a sky 'just as wide as the one back home' and a neighbor growing tomatoes. The turning point is pushing open the roof door and seeing the wide sky and the neighbor's words, 'You just have to come up and look,' after which he starts going up most evenings and no longer wants to leave.

steps: Show the setting creating the conflict: the move takes 'his old street, his friends, the wide quiet sky,' and the apartment faces 'a brick wall' with constant noise, so Amir decides to be miserable.
Find the turning point in the setting: pushing open the roof door and seeing 'a sky just as wide as the one back home,' plus the neighbor's line 'You just have to come up and look.'
Show the setting resolving the conflict: the roof, tomatoes, bakery, and chess game make the city 'a place he did not want to leave.'
Connect: the same city that caused his misery, seen from the roof, becomes the source of his change, so the setting both creates and resolves the conflict.

Read the passage, then answer the question.

Lena's grandmother had given her an old pocket watch, and Lena wore it every day. It did not keep good time, running a few minutes slow, but Lena loved the soft tick of it. Then, at the start of sixth grade, a popular girl named Whitney laughed at it. "That thing is ancient," she said. The other kids laughed too. The next morning, Lena left the watch in her drawer.

For a month the watch stayed in the dark. Lena felt lighter at school, blending in, until the afternoon her grandmother asked, gently, why she never wore it anymore. Lena said she had been afraid of losing it. It was the first lie she had ever told her grandmother, and it sat in her stomach all night.

The next day was the school's history fair. Each student was supposed to bring an object that told a story. Lena had planned to bring a printed photo. But that morning, standing at her drawer, she took out the watch instead and clasped it on.

At the fair she explained how the watch had belonged to her grandmother, who had carried it through two big moves and a war, and how it ran slow because it had been ticking for seventy years. The room got quiet in a way Whitney's laughter never had. Afterward, even Whitney came over to look at it. Walking home, Lena felt the familiar slow tick against her wrist and understood she had almost traded something real for the feeling of blending in.

Identify the turning point that changes Lena's decision about the watch, and explain how the resolution differs from her state at the beginning. Use evidence from the text.
items.answer: The turning point is the lie Lena tells her grandmother about being afraid of losing the watch, which 'sat in her stomach all night' and pushes her, the next morning at the history fair, to clasp the watch on instead of bringing the planned photo. At the beginning Lena hides the watch in her drawer to blend in after Whitney's laughter. By the resolution she proudly wears and explains the watch, understanding she 'had almost traded something real for the feeling of blending in,' showing she now values the watch over fitting in.

steps: Identify the beginning state: after Whitney laughs, Lena leaves the watch 'in her drawer' to blend in.
Find the turning point: lying to her grandmother, which 'sat in her stomach all night' and is 'the first lie she had ever told.'
Trace the decision change: the next morning she 'took out the watch instead' of the photo and wears it to the fair.
Contrast the resolution with the start: she ends up valuing the watch over blending in, realizing she 'almost traded something real,' a reversal of her earlier choice.

The canoe trip was supposed to last three days, but on the second afternoon, dark clouds stacked up over the lake faster than the guide had predicted. Twelve-year-old Sam was in a canoe with his cousin Reyes when the wind hit. Waves slapped over the sides. The guide shouted for everyone to head for the nearest island.

Sam had always let Reyes take charge. Reyes was older, louder, the one who made the plans. But now Reyes froze, gripping his paddle, eyes wide. The shore was getting no closer. Sam felt the same fear, but he also felt the canoe drifting sideways into the waves, and he knew that was the worst thing that could happen.

"Match my strokes," Sam said, surprising himself. "Left, now left, now left." He kept his voice even, calling the rhythm, and after a frozen second Reyes started to paddle with him. Together they turned the bow into the waves and pushed toward the island. It took everything they had, but they made it to the rocks just as the rain came down in sheets.

Under the shelter of a pine, soaked and shaking, Reyes looked at Sam differently. "How did you know what to do?" he asked. Sam wasn't sure. He had spent his whole life following. But in the moment when following wasn't an option, he had found he could lead. After the storm passed, when they paddled out again, it was Sam who set the pace.

Explain how the storm setting forces Sam's change, and identify the climax of the story. Use evidence from the text.
items.answer: The storm forces Sam's change by making following impossible: Reyes, who 'made the plans,' freezes, and the canoe drifts 'sideways into the waves,' so Sam must act. The climax is Sam taking command and calling the rhythm, 'Match my strokes... Left, now left,' which turns the canoe into the waves and toward the island. This is the climax because it is the highest tension point where the conflict (surviving the storm) turns toward resolution and where Sam changes from a lifelong follower into someone who 'could lead,' shown afterward when 'it was Sam who set the pace.'

steps: Show the setting forcing change: the sudden storm and Reyes freezing leave Sam, who 'had always let Reyes take charge,' as the only one who can act.
Identify the climax: Sam calling 'Match my strokes' and steering the canoe into the waves, the peak of tension as they fight toward the island.
Justify it as the turning point: the conflict (survival) turns here, and Sam's character flips from follower to leader.
Confirm with the resolution: after the storm 'it was Sam who set the pace,' showing the change the climax produced.

Read the passage, then answer the question.

Juniper had spent two years convinced her older brother, Cole, had stopped caring about her. When he left for high school, the easy afternoons of him helping with her bike or her homework simply ended. He came home late, headphones in, and barely looked up. She decided he had outgrown her and built a wall of her own, answering him as coldly as she felt he treated her.

The winter Cole turned sixteen, their father went into the hospital for surgery. The house went quiet and tense. Juniper expected Cole to disappear into his room as usual. Instead, the first night, he knocked on her door and asked if she wanted to watch the movies they used to watch as little kids. She was too surprised to say no.

He did it every night their father was gone. He made the bad popcorn they both liked. He helped with her homework again, clumsily, out of practice. One night she finally asked why he had been ignoring her for two years. Cole looked genuinely confused. "I thought you didn't want a babyish brother hanging around," he said. "You stopped asking me for stuff."

Juniper sat with that. Both of them had built the same wall, each thinking the other one started it. When their father came home, healing well, Cole drifted toward his own life again, but differently now. He left his door open. He still made the popcorn on weekends. Juniper had stopped believing he didn't care, because she finally understood the silence had never meant what she thought.

Explain the misunderstanding at the center of the conflict and identify the turning point that resolves it. Use evidence from the text.
items.answer: The central misunderstanding is that both Juniper and Cole 'built the same wall, each thinking the other one started it': Juniper believed Cole 'had outgrown her,' while Cole thought she 'didn't want a babyish brother hanging around' because she 'stopped asking.' The turning point is the father's hospital stay, which prompts Cole to knock on her door and restart their old routine, and especially the night Juniper asks why he ignored her and Cole reveals his confusion. By the resolution she stops believing he didn't care, understanding 'the silence had never meant what she thought.'

steps: Identify the conflict: Juniper's belief that Cole 'stopped caring,' which made her build 'a wall of her own.'
Find the hidden truth: Cole thought she 'stopped asking' because she didn't want him around, so both built 'the same wall.'
Locate the turning point: the father's surgery brings Cole to her door, and her direct question reveals the misunderstanding.
State the resolution: she 'stopped believing he didn't care' once she understood 'the silence had never meant what she thought.'

Read the passage, then answer the question.

The village of Hollow Pine sat at the bottom of a valley, and every spring the snowmelt swelled the river that ran through it. For generations the villagers had relied on a single wooden bridge to reach the market town on the far bank. Tam, the blacksmith's daughter, crossed it twice a week and never thought about it, until the spring the river rose higher than anyone living could remember.

The water clawed at the bridge supports. One morning Tam watched a whole section of railing tear away and spin downstream. The villagers gathered on the bank, arguing. Some wanted to wait and hope the bridge held. Others said it was already lost. Tam noticed that while they argued, no one was actually doing anything, and the water kept rising.

She remembered her father saying that a chain is only as strong as its weakest link. She walked the near bank until she found where the current pushed hardest against the bridge, and she saw that one support, not the whole bridge, was failing first. She ran to tell the adults, but they waved her off as a child. So she gathered the other children, and together they hauled stones to brace that single support, working in a chain, passing rocks hand to hand.

By the time the adults stopped arguing and came to look, the children had reinforced the weak point, and the bridge held through the flood. When the water finally fell, the village still had its only crossing. Tam, who had crossed that bridge a thousand times without a thought, never crossed it again the same way.

Explain how the setting drives the conflict and how Tam's understanding lets her solve it, and identify the climax. Use evidence from the text.
items.answer: The valley setting drives the conflict because Hollow Pine sits 'at the bottom of a valley' where spring snowmelt swells the river, and the village depends on 'a single wooden bridge,' so the rising flood threatens their only crossing. Tam solves it by recalling that 'a chain is only as strong as its weakest link' and spotting that one support 'was failing first,' then bracing that single point. The climax is the children hauling stones to reinforce the weak support 'in a chain,' the high-tension effort that decides whether the bridge survives, and it holds 'through the flood.'

steps: Connect setting to conflict: the valley location and spring snowmelt swell the river, and the village relies on 'a single wooden bridge,' so the flood endangers their only link to the market town.
Show Tam's key insight: her father's saying about the 'weakest link' lets her see that 'one support, not the whole bridge, was failing first.'
Identify the climax: the children hauling and passing stones 'hand to hand' to brace the weak support, the peak action that determines the outcome.
Confirm the resolution: the bridge 'held through the flood' and the village keeps its crossing, completing the arc.

Read the passage, then answer the question.

Every summer Priya visited her aunt's bakery and dreamed of decorating the grand wedding cakes in the window. This summer her aunt finally said yes, she could decorate one cake for a real order. Priya pictured something perfect. She practiced for a week.

On the morning of the order, her hand slipped, and a long crack split the smooth white frosting down one side. Her stomach dropped. She thought about hiding it, turning the cracked side to the wall, hoping no one would look. For a moment she even considered telling her aunt the order had been cancelled.

But her aunt had trusted her. So Priya took a breath and did the opposite of hiding. She studied the crack. Then, instead of covering it, she made it a feature, piping a trail of sugar flowers that grew right out of the split, as if the cake had cracked open to bloom. She worked slowly, turning the flaw into a vine of blossoms that wound up the whole side.

When the customer arrived, she gasped, not at a mistake, but at the design. She said it was the most original cake she had ever seen and asked who had made it. Priya's aunt pointed at her. Priya, who that morning had wanted to hide a crack and lie about it, understood that the cake was better for the flaw than it would have been if nothing had gone wrong. She had stopped trying to be perfect and started trying to be honest.

Describe how Priya changes from the beginning of the story to the resolution, and identify the turning point that prompts the change. Use evidence from the text.
items.answer: Priya's first impulse is to hide the cracked frosting, even considering lying that the order was cancelled, because she wanted the cake to be perfect. By the resolution she has changed: she turns the flaw into 'a vine of blossoms' rather than concealing it, and she understands the cake 'was better for the flaw' and that she 'had stopped trying to be perfect and started trying to be honest.' The turning point is the thought that 'her aunt had trusted her,' which makes Priya choose to study the crack and 'do the opposite of hiding.'

steps: Identify the beginning impulse: Priya wants to hide the crack, 'turning the cracked side to the wall,' and even thinks about lying that the order was cancelled.
Find the turning point: 'But her aunt had trusted her,' which leads her to 'do the opposite of hiding' and study the crack.
Trace the action: she pipes flowers 'right out of the split,' turning the flaw into a feature.

State the change: she stops 'trying to be perfect' and starts 'trying to be honest,' realizing the cake was 'better for the flaw.' Note the question asks how Priya changes and what the turning point is.

The lighthouse on Crane Point had been automated for years, but old Mr. Halloran still lived in the keeper's cottage beside it, and twelve-year-old Wren brought him groceries every Friday. She thought of him as cranky and dull. He rarely spoke, and when he did, it was usually to complain about the weather.

One Friday a storm rolled in early, and the automated light failed, just as a small fishing boat was trying to find the harbor in the dark. Wren expected Mr. Halloran to shrug, the way he shrugged at everything. Instead, the old man moved faster than she had ever seen him. He climbed the lighthouse stairs, and when the electric light would not start, he pulled out an oil lamp older than Wren's grandmother, lit it, and held it in the window, turning it slowly so the boat could fix on the rhythm.

Wren held the matches and watched his face. He was not cranky now. He was focused, murmuring counts under his breath, the way he must have done a thousand times before the light was automated. The fishing boat found the harbor. Only when its lights reached the dock did Mr. Halloran sit down, suddenly old again.

Walking home, Wren thought about how she had decided who he was after months of groceries and small talk, and how wrong she had been. The cranky man complaining about weather had been a keeper all along, just waiting for a night the machines failed. She never brought the groceries the same way again.

Explain how the storm reveals a different side of Mr. Halloran, and explain why this is a change in Wren rather than in him. Use evidence from the text.
items.answer: The storm reveals Mr. Halloran as a skilled, devoted keeper rather than a cranky old man: when the automated light fails he 'moved faster than she had ever seen him,' lights an old oil lamp, and turns it 'so the boat could fix on the rhythm,' murmuring practiced counts. This is a change in Wren, not in him, because he 'had been a keeper all along,' just waiting for a night the machines failed. What changes is Wren's understanding: she realizes how 'wrong she had been' to decide who he was, and she 'never brought the groceries the same way again.'

steps: Note Wren's initial judgment: she thinks Mr. Halloran is 'cranky and dull,' someone who only complains about weather.
Show what the storm reveals: he lights the old oil lamp and guides the boat in, focused and expert, 'the way he must have done a thousand times.'
Explain why he does not change: the text says he 'had been a keeper all along,' so this side already existed; the storm only exposes it.
Identify Wren's change: she sees how 'wrong she had been' and treats him differently, so the real change is in her perception.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer the question.

Oscar had built the same routine for two years to avoid one thing: speaking in class. He sat in the back, kept his eyes down, and let the words pile up in his head, unsaid. Teachers marked him as shy. He told himself he simply had nothing to add.

Then Ms. Reyes assigned a debate, and she paired Oscar with the topic he cared about most: whether the city should save the old library down the street, the one where he had spent every rainy afternoon of his childhood. The other side, two confident students, argued it was a waste of money. Oscar listened to them describe the building as useless, and the unsaid words in his head began to push harder than his fear.

When his turn came, his voice shook on the first sentence. But he had walked those library shelves a hundred times, and once he started describing them, the trembling steadied. He talked about the reading nook by the window, the librarian who knew every kid's name, the books that had pulled him through a hard year. He forgot to be afraid because he was too busy meaning what he said.

When he finished, the room was silent, then it broke into applause, and even the other team nodded. Oscar sat down shaking again, but for a different reason now. He had spent two years believing he had nothing to add. The truth, he saw, was that he had simply never cared enough to push through the fear, and now he had.

Explain what Oscar believed about himself at the start, identify the turning point that breaks that belief, and describe what he actually learns. Use evidence from the text.
items.answer: At the start Oscar believes he 'simply had nothing to add,' using his routine to avoid speaking and letting teachers mark him as shy. The turning point comes during the debate when the other side calls the old library 'useless,' so 'the unsaid words in his head began to push harder than his fear,' and he speaks about the library he loves until 'the trembling steadied.' What he actually learns is that he never lacked things to say: 'he had simply never cared enough to push through the fear,' and now, caring about the library, he could.

steps: Identify Oscar's starting belief: he tells himself he 'simply had nothing to add' and avoids speaking.
Find the turning point: hearing the library called 'useless' makes 'the unsaid words' push 'harder than his fear,' driving him to speak.
Track the change in the moment: his voice shakes, then steadies once he describes the library he loves, and he 'forgot to be afraid.'
State what he learns: the real issue was never having 'nothing to add' but never having 'cared enough to push through the fear,' which the library topic changes.
